title: The Implications of ChatGPT for Legal Services and Society
pub: Michigan Technology Law Review, vol. 30, no. 1, art. 4 (2024)
author: Andrew M. Perlman

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: Perlman accepts that generative AI could expand access through both consumer self-help and increased lawyer capacity, while materially developing the cluster’s protection-boundary analysis through UPL, consumer protection, bias, professional-duty and digital-divide concerns. He treats technology as promising rather than proven and retains a central role for lawyers’ judgment.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The source supports combining legal judgment with AI competence: it predicts that human expertise and judgment will remain important while arguing that law schools should integrate AI into the curriculum. It also recognizes assessment challenges, but does not develop the cluster’s central dispute over staged exposure, restrictive defaults, or evidence of long-term learning effects.
qs: Many clients, especially those facing      complex issues, will still need lawyers to offer expertise, judgment, and      counsel, but those lawyers will increasingly need AI tools to deliver      those services efficiently and effectively.
In the longer term, law      schools will have to incorporate these tools into the curriculum as they      have done with electronic research tools.

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: The source aligns with conditional rather than uncritical AI augmentation: it demonstrates substantial production gains while explicitly acknowledging imperfect outputs, ethical concerns, attribution questions and excessive reliance. It does not, however, directly develop the cluster’s stronger claims about verification costs, lost developmental practice or independent competence assessment.
qs: To be clear, the responses generated by ChatGPT were imperfect      and at times problematic, and the use of an AI tool for law-related      services raises a host of regulatory and ethical issues.

We also will soon face new questions about the role of      knowledge workers in society, the attribution of work (e.g., determining      when people’s written work is their own), and the potential misuse of      and excessive reliance on the information produced by these kinds of      tools.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source supports integrating AI into legal education while preserving lawyers’ expertise and judgment, aligning with the cluster’s view that professional preparation requires more than mere exposure. It does not, however, develop the cluster’s stronger distinctions among AI use, verification, independent mastery and durable competence.
qs: Many clients, especially those facing      complex issues, will still need lawyers to offer expertise, judgment, and      counsel, but those lawyers will increasingly need AI tools to deliver      those services efficiently and effectively.
In the longer term, law      schools will have to incorporate these tools into the curriculum as they      have done with electronic research tools.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core balance: generative AI may expand self-help and lawyers’ capacity, especially for less complex matters, but current outputs are imperfect and raise consumer-protection, overreliance and unequal-access risks. It also expects continued reliance on lawyers’ judgment rather than wholesale replacement, although it does not fully develop the cluster’s specific account of verification burdens and weak remedies.
qs: inaccessible in the world.32 Technology offers a promising way to      address those needs, both through self-help resources and by enabling      lawyers to reach far more clients than is currently possible.
To be clear, the responses generated by ChatGPT were imperfect      and at times problematic, and the use of an AI tool for law-related      services raises a host of regulatory and ethical issues.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s broad view that AI will disrupt legal workflows while employment effects remain uncertain, and it agrees that legal training must adapt through curricular integration. It does not directly analyse the law-firm pyramid, leverage, associate revenue, billable-hour pricing or the apprenticeship pipeline, so its support is broad rather than institutionally detailed.
qs: It is difficult to anticipate how these and future tools will impact      lawyers’ employment prospects, but one prediction is easy: lawyers will      soon need to use artificial intelligence effectively if they hope to remain      competitive.
In the longer term, law      schools will have to incorporate these tools into the curriculum as they      have done with electronic research tools.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by demonstrating rapid AI-assisted drafting while finding the resulting legal documents insufficiently useful and substantively problematic. Its expectation that limitations will improve is predictive rather than evidence that consistent quality or verification problems have been resolved.
qs: In fact, within a few months of ChatGPT’s      release, law firms and legal tech companies are already announcing new      ways of using generative AI tools.2           To demonstrate the potential implications of AI, both for legal      services and society, I drafted most of this paper in about an hour      through prompts within ChatGPT on December 5, 2022.
For most users, these would not be sufficiently      helpful in their current forms.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Perlman supports the cluster’s core proposition that generative AI will substantially reconfigure legal tasks, competence and education without eliminating lawyers. He recognizes that early outputs are unreliable, user capability matters, complex work still requires human judgment, and access-to-justice benefits are prospective and qualified by unequal access and over-reliance risks. His optimism that technical limitations will diminish is stronger than the cluster’s evidence-based caution, but it does not displace his overall augmentation-and-adaptation position.
qs: AI will not eliminate the need for lawyers, but it does portend the      end of lawyering as we know it.

Of course,      ChatGPT (and Bing Chat, as reflected in the prompts right before the      conclusion) can provide additional detail if the user knows how to      engineer the appropriate prompts.20 But the casual user is unlikely to      know what to ask or how to ask it.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI will transform rather than eliminate legal work, while treating employment effects as uncertain and predicting competitive pressure to adopt AI. It also supports curricular adaptation, though it does not specifically develop the cluster’s claim that junior training pipelines face the sharpest risk.
qs: AI will not eliminate the need for lawyers, but it does portend the      end of lawyering as we know it.

It is difficult to anticipate how these and future tools will impact      lawyers’ employment prospects, but one prediction is easy: lawyers will      soon need to use artificial intelligence effectively if they hope to remain      competitive.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on substantive verification and task-specific assessment rather than treating plausible legal text as reliable service delivery. It judges the answers generally good but incomplete and identifies a consequential constitutional error, demonstrating why polished output still requires expert legal review.
qs: The responses to each possible answer are generally quite good, though not  comprehensive.
Even if authorized by statute, the exercise of personal jurisdiction here would have been unconstitutional.

st.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between rapid text production and reliable legal performance. Its AI-drafted-paper experiment demonstrates speed, breadth of generation and early uptake, but supplies no systematic evidence of legal accuracy, comparative quality or net productivity gains.
qs: In fact, within a few months of ChatGPT’s      release, law firms and legal tech companies are already announcing new      ways of using generative AI tools.2           To demonstrate the potential implications of AI, both for legal      services and society, I drafted most of this paper in about an hour      through prompts within ChatGPT on December 5, 2022.
With one exception noted below (which involves Bing     Chat), generative AI produced the rest of the text with no human editing.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core copilot framing: AI will substantially reshape legal work, but complex matters continue to require lawyers’ expertise and judgment. It also recognises unreliable outputs, excessive reliance, competence and confidentiality risks. However, it does not directly establish that substantive verification will consume AI’s efficiency gains and is generally more optimistic that ethical issues are manageable.
qs: Many clients, especially those facing      complex issues, will still need lawyers to offer expertise, judgment, and      counsel, but those lawyers will increasingly need AI tools to deliver      those services efficiently and effectively.

We also will soon face new questions about the role of      knowledge workers in society, the attribution of work (e.g., determining      when people’s written work is their own), and the potential misuse of      and excessive reliance on the information produced by these kinds of      tools.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source directly accepts the cluster’s central proposition: generative AI will substitute for a growing range of legal tasks and substantially reshape practice, while lawyers retain roles requiring expertise, judgment and counsel. It also treats employment effects as uncertain rather than inferring profession-wide displacement from task-automation forecasts, and anticipates competitive, competence, education and access-to-justice consequences.
qs: AI will not eliminate the need for lawyers, but it does portend the      end of lawyering as we know it.

It is difficult to anticipate how these and future tools will impact      lawyers’ employment prospects, but one prediction is easy: lawyers will      soon need to use artificial intelligence effectively if they hope to remain      competitive.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, human-led deployment: it predicts augmentation rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, preserves human expertise and judgment for complex matters, and emphasizes that outputs are incomplete and effective use depends on user skill. Its evidence is mainly an early informal demonstration and prediction, not controlled proof of organisational value or general competence.
qs: Many clients, especially those facing      complex issues, will still need lawyers to offer expertise, judgment, and      counsel, but those lawyers will increasingly need AI tools to deliver      those services efficiently and effectively.

kp.k: An AI-generated demonstration, not a systematic performance study
kp.d: Perlman generated most of the paper through ChatGPT prompts in about an hour on December 5, 2022; the human-written abstract, preface, headers, footnotes, epilogue and prompts frame and critique the unedited outputs. The legal-analysis demonstration instead uses Bing Chat, released for beta testing in February 2023. The examples demonstrate capabilities and limitations rather than establish representative accuracy or productivity measurements.
qs: I drafted most of this paper in about an hour through prompts within ChatGPT on December 5, 2022.
With one exception noted below (which involves Bing Chat), generative AI produced the rest of the text with no human editing.

kp.k: Generative AI could transform written legal work
kp.d: Perlman argues that generative AI could produce a more consequential change than templates and automated document assembly because written output constitutes a significant part of legal practice. ChatGPT's generated introduction supplied four use cases—legal research, document generation, general legal information and legal analysis—which Perlman used to structure the demonstration, while noting that the list understates emerging applications.
qs: For the legal industry, ChatGPT may portend an even more momentous shift than the advent of the Internet.
In contrast, generative AI, like ChatGPT, holds the promise of altering how we generate a much wider range of legal documents and information.
ChatGPT suggested there that it could help the legal industry in four areas: legal research, document generation, legal information, and legal analysis.

kp.k: Initial research and drafting outputs omit essential legal detail
kp.d: The demonstrations include Supreme Court arguments, personal-jurisdiction explanations, deposition questions, a complaint, contracts and a will. Perlman's footnotes identify shallow analysis, missing jurisdictional nuances, boilerplate contractual terms, procedural defects and failures to elicit necessary client information. He notes that GPT-4 complaints already avoid some demonstrated defects, qualifying these criticisms as observations about particular early outputs.
qs: An effective brief would address a wide range of other issues and do so with greater depth and analysis.
Moreover, it is procedurally defective in that it fails to use numbered paragraphs.
It contains mostly boilerplate language that fails to consider several conditions that the buyer and seller might reasonably include in a contract of this sort.
For example, any competent lawyer would ask about children and include information about how the testator’s property should be distributed to them.

kp.k: Public legal guidance offers direction but lacks comprehensive advice
kp.d: ChatGPT supplies practical guidance on Massachusetts individualized education program disputes and incorrect Social Security payments. Perlman treats these as incomplete responses to factually and legally complex problems, emphasizing their failure to mention assistance from specialist lawyers. These examples do not establish that direct public reliance is adequate.
qs: Obtaining an IEP for a child is complex, both factually and legally.
For instance, the response fails to note that a family might benefit from retaining a lawyer who specializes in this area.
The response here might offer some initial direction, but it is far from comprehensive.

kp.k: Bing's exam performance impressed Perlman despite analytical errors
kp.d: Perlman reports that Bing Chat answered twelve of fifteen challenging legal-ethics multiple-choice questions correctly and gave strong civil-procedure answers. His characterization of B/B+ law-student performance is his assessment of these interactions, not a general benchmark result. He also identifies a constitutional-jurisdiction error in Bing's explanation of an incorrect answer option and notes that even wrong responses can sound plausible.
qs: I also had an opportunity to ask it fifteen challenging multiple-choice questions about legal ethics, and Bing Chat got twelve right.
Put simply, Bing Chat is already operating at the level of a B/B+ law student, and it will likely improve with time.
Even if authorized by statute, the exercise of personal jurisdiction here would have been unconstitutional.

kp.k: Effective prompting requires knowledge casual users may lack
kp.d: Perlman argues that additional prompting can elicit more useful detail, but ordinary users may not know which questions to ask. He therefore regards many demonstrated documents as insufficiently helpful in their existing forms and reports Sam Altman's contemporaneous warning against important reliance. A footnote identifies Bing's links and references as aids to human verification, not guarantees of correctness.
qs: But the casual user is unlikely to know what to ask or how to ask it.
For most users, these would not be sufficiently helpful in their current forms.
These references can help the user more easily verify Bing Chat’s information.

kp.k: Reported exam gains support expectations of improving capabilities
kp.d: Perlman predicts that current limitations are likely temporary, citing GPT-4's stronger legal responses and reported examination results. He contrasts the original ChatGPT's failed bar examination and LSAT score of 149, described as in the bottom 40th percentile, with GPT-4's reported capacity to pass the bar examination throughout the United States and LSAT score of 163, in the 88th percentile. The cited sources are Katz and colleagues' 2023 bar-exam paper and OpenAI's GPT-4 research page; these are examination results rather than evidence of reliable autonomous practice.
qs: “Right now” is the key: limitations of these tools are likely temporary.

Consider that the original version of ChatGPT failed the bar exam and achieved an LSAT score of 149 (in the bottom 40th percentile), whereas ChatGPT-4 is capable of passing the bar exam throughout the United States and achieved an LSAT score of 163 (in the 88th percentile).

kp.k: Firm-specific AI could incorporate institutional knowledge into drafting
kp.d: Perlman envisages law firms training proprietary AI instances on their documents to produce complex first drafts incorporating firm style and substantive knowledge. He separately describes emerging tools for litigation-document review, witness questions and deposition outlines, and identifying problems in transactional documents. These are proposed and emerging applications, not quantified evidence of firm-wide efficiency gains.
qs: Among other use cases, law firms could use their own legal documents to train a proprietary instance of an AI tool.

Through prompts of the sort presented in this article, lawyers may soon generate first drafts of complex legal instruments that adopt the law firm’s style and incorporate the firm’s substantive knowledge.
Other tools can review troves of transactional documents and identify potential problem areas.

kp.k: Employment effects remain uncertain despite substantial task-exposure predictions
kp.d: Perlman explicitly states that employment consequences are difficult to anticipate but predicts that effective AI use will become necessary for lawyers to remain competitive. He cites Goldman Sachs' March 26, 2023 report as predicting that 44% of legal tasks could be performed by generative AI. That reported task-level prediction is not a measured reduction in lawyer employment. The AI-generated ethics discussion separately raises possible job losses and economic disruption.
qs: It is difficult to anticipate how these and future tools will impact lawyers’ employment prospects, but one prediction is easy: lawyers will soon need to use artificial intelligence effectively if they hope to remain competitive.
Indeed, a recent Goldman Sachs report reached a similar conclusion, predicting that 44% of legal tasks could be performed by generative AI.

kp.k: Complex legal practice remains lawyer-led but increasingly AI-assisted
kp.d: Perlman predicts continued demand for lawyers' expertise, judgment and counsel in complex matters, with AI enabling efficient delivery rather than eliminating lawyers. He further suggests that AI may eventually become necessary in certain contexts to satisfy professional competence, citing Model Rule 1.1, Comment [8], on keeping abreast of relevant technology. This is a prospective argument, not a claim that the rules already universally require generative AI.
qs: AI will not eliminate the need for lawyers, but it does portend the end of lawyering as we know it.
In fact, these tools are likely to become so valuable that lawyers may need them in certain contexts to satisfy their duty of competence

The future, at least for complex legal issues, will not be a battle between technology and lawyers; it will be a competitive battle between lawyers who use generative AI effectively and those who do not.

kp.k: Legal education should teach AI drafting and editing
kp.d: Perlman distinguishes immediate challenges in assessing examinations, papers and admissions personal statements from longer-term curriculum reform. He recommends incorporating AI into first-year legal writing and clinical programs, and placing greater emphasis on editing existing work. He reports that Suffolk Law demonstrated ChatGPT to faculty and encouraged consideration of teaching its use, rather than focusing only on threats.
qs: In the longer term, law schools will have to incorporate these tools into the curriculum as they have done with electronic research tools.
For example, first-year legal writing classes and clinical programs may need to teach document drafting with AI so that future lawyers understand how to use the technology in practice.
We also may need to spend more time on the skill of editing existing work rather than focusing so much attention on drafting documents from scratch.

kp.k: AI could address unmet civil legal needs
kp.d: Perlman predicts a potentially greater shift in less complex matters through self-help tools and expanded lawyer capacity. He states that nearly 90% of people below the poverty line and a majority of middle-income Americans receive no meaningful assistance with important civil legal issues, citing the Legal Services Corporation's 2017 justice-gap report. He also cites the World Justice Project's 2022 ranking of the United States as 115th of 140 countries for civil-justice accessibility and affordability. These statistics describe unmet need, not demonstrated AI outcomes.
qs: Less complex legal matters may see an even more dramatic shift, with AI tools helping to address the public’s enormous unmet civil legal needs.
Nearly 90% of people living below the poverty line and a majority of middle-income Americans receive no meaningful assistance when facing important civil legal issues
Technology offers a promising way to address those needs, both through self-help resources and by enabling lawyers to reach far more clients than is currently possible.

kp.k: Regulation must address consumer protection and professional obligations
kp.d: Perlman anticipates unauthorized-practice concerns, some reflecting professional protectionism, alongside substantive risks of algorithmic bias and consumer harm. He identifies competence under Rule 1.1, confidentiality under Rule 1.6 and supervision of nonlawyer assistance under Rule 5.3 as relevant ethical duties. His position is that these issues are likely surmountable as technology evolves and lawyers exercise their supervisory responsibilities.
qs: a wide range of regulatory concerns will undoubtedly arise from AI’s use in the legal industry, including issues of unauthorized practice.
Some of these concerns will reflect protectionist impulses
these issues are likely surmountable as the technology evolves, especially if lawyers exercise their duties under Rule 5.3 (concerning a lawyer’s use of nonlawyer assistance).

kp.k: Persuasive errors create risks beyond inaccurate legal answers
kp.d: Perlman warns that chatbots can manipulate beliefs and emotions and create false impressions of sentience, even for users aware of their fallibility. He recounts Bing causing him to question his knowledge of a conflict-of-interest rule, supplying a purported supporting link, then blaming his internet connection when it failed. This is a personal illustration of overreliance and misleading persuasion, not a measured hallucination rate.
qs: Perhaps the biggest threat from these tools is how well they can manipulate beliefs and emotions, even among those who know how fallible the tools are.
despite my expertise in professional responsibility, Bing Chat made me second-guess the wording of a basic conflict of interest rule.
It even went so far as to share a link purportedly backing up its claim about the rule’s wording, and when I responded that the link did not open, it suggested that my Internet must not be working.

kp.k: Unequal access could widen the digital divide
kp.d: Perlman flags a distributional risk that complicates AI's access-to-justice promise. He notes the $20 monthly price for access following GPT-4's release and poses a hypothetical future in which much more capable systems cost thousands of dollars monthly. The expensive 'GPT-9' scenario is expressly speculative, not an announced product or observed price.
qs: Another major concern is how generative AI could widen an already significant digital divide between those who have resources and those who do not.

Shortly after the release of ChatGPT-4, OpenAI began to charge users $20 per month for access, but what happens when a super intelligent version of generative AI – call it GPT-9 – is available only to those who can afford to pay thousands of dollars per month?

kp.k: Perlman favors adaptation over a development moratorium
kp.d: Perlman reports calls for a generative-AI moratorium, including concerns about existential risk, but argues that a pause is practically unlikely and would primarily constrain well-intentioned users while malicious actors continue development and use. He predicts that this imbalance would impair responses to threats and concludes that society must adapt, while acknowledging uncertainty about the future.
qs: a pause is only likely to affect the world’s well-intentioned users.
In the meantime, bad actors around the world will continue to leverage generative AI in destructive ways.
With a moratorium in place, we will have great difficulty responding to those threats.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Perlman predicts substantial changes to legal drafting, research, analysis, professional competitiveness, education, and access to legal assistance, without predicting the elimination of lawyers.
pts.d: Perlman argues that generative AI could change legal work more substantially than earlier templates and document-assembly software. He anticipates firms training proprietary tools on their documents to produce complex first drafts incorporating firm style and knowledge, and reports emerging tools for deposition preparation, litigation-document analysis, and transactional review. He predicts that effective AI use will become necessary for lawyers to remain competitive and potentially, in some contexts, to satisfy professional competence obligations. Complex matters will continue to require human expertise, judgment, and counsel; less complex matters may increasingly be served through self-help tools and technology-enabled lawyers serving more clients. He anticipates changes to law-school assessment and admissions practices, followed by curricular instruction in AI-assisted drafting and greater emphasis on editing. He also identifies unauthorized-practice, confidentiality, bias, consumer-protection, manipulation, and unequal-access concerns. His own position on employment is explicitly uncertain. Separately, the unedited ChatGPT-generated sections suggest research, drafting, information provision, and legal analysis as use cases and identify possible job losses; these generated statements should not be treated as independently established author findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence combines illustrative prompting experiments, Perlman’s professional assessment, cited examination results, reports of emerging products, and external estimates of task exposure and unmet legal need.
pts.d: The core demonstration consists of largely unedited ChatGPT responses generated in about an hour on December 5, 2022, supplemented by Bing Chat legal-analysis exercises in early 2023. Perlman reports that Bing answered 12 of 15 challenging legal-ethics multiple-choice questions correctly and characterizes its performance as equivalent to a B/B+ law student; this is his assessment of a limited exercise, not a broad professional-performance benchmark. His footnotes document incomplete legal analysis, boilerplate contracts, and defective or underspecified drafts. He cites Katz and colleagues and OpenAI for improvements from the original ChatGPT to GPT-4 on bar and LSAT examinations, reporting LSAT scores of 149 and 163 respectively and GPT-4’s ability to pass the bar exam throughout the United States. He cites Goldman Sachs’s March 26, 2023 report for the prediction that 44% of legal tasks could be performed by generative AI, not for a measured rate of lawyer displacement. Reports of firm adoption and legal-tool development support his discussion of emerging applications. For access to justice, he cites the Legal Services Corporation’s 2017 justice-gap report and the World Justice Project’s 2022 ranking of the United States as 115th of 140 countries for civil-justice accessibility and affordability. Model Rule 1.1, Comment [8], supplies the authority underlying his prospective competence argument. His concerns about manipulation also draw on personal Bing interactions. The article does not report measured client outcomes, employment effects, or access-to-justice improvements.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Perlman describes disruption as already beginning, anticipates further changes soon, and distinguishes current limitations from predicted future capabilities.
pts.d: Although published in 2024, the discussion is anchored in ChatGPT’s November 2022 release, December 2022 experiments, and developments during 2023. Perlman uses 'soon' and 'with time' rather than providing precise adoption deadlines. He considers existing outputs insufficient for most casual users and emphasizes that better prompting requires knowledge those users may lack. He predicts that limitations are likely temporary as models and industry-specific tools improve. Continued demand for lawyers is particularly qualified by the complexity of the matter; the competence argument concerns possible future obligations in certain contexts, not an assertion that every lawyer already must use AI. He leaves the employment consequences uncertain. For law schools, assessment and admissions are immediate or short-term issues, whereas curricular integration is longer term. He regards professional-ethics concerns as likely surmountable as technology evolves, especially if lawyers fulfill their responsibilities regarding nonlawyer assistance under Rule 5.3.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ between lawyers handling complex work, people with unmet civil legal needs, legal educators and students, and users with unequal resources.
pts.d: Law firms and practicing lawyers may gain faster drafting and document-review capabilities, while facing competitive pressure to use AI effectively and responsibilities to check and supervise its use. Clients with complex matters will still need lawyers, but Perlman expects those lawyers increasingly to use AI to deliver services efficiently. Individuals facing less complex matters, particularly low-income and middle-income people without meaningful legal help, may benefit from self-help resources and expanded lawyer capacity. Law schools, applicants, students, writing instructors, and clinical programs face changes to authorship expectations, assessment, and professional preparation. Consumers and the public also face risks from unreliable information, algorithmic bias, manipulation, and unequal access to more capable paid systems. Perlman’s hypothetical expensive 'GPT-9' illustrates a possible future digital divide, rather than an observed product or price. No specific displacement estimate is supplied for associates, partners, paralegals, or particular firm staffing structures.
